exclusions.A: Marrow's boards earned their place on those stairs.
exclusions.B: He gave the U of Upper Gate a long tail and the L of Lower Gate a heavy foot, and in four decades the crews never once mixed up the two Gates, even at night.
exclusions.C: Every driver who reaches Hollins Ford after dark still finds the way by letters he drew on Tanner Street, and the foundry did well to copy them line for line.
exclusions.D: They spent a fortnight in storage at the depot shed and then went up in street order, one landing at a time.

support: Marrow's boards earned their place on those stairs.
The care in those patterns shows best at the Gates, two of the first boards he painted.
WV12-P01.5.note: The author praises the boards' care, legibility and durability and says they earned their place, with no irony and no lament since the letters live on in the new signs.

exclusions.A: Her two hives stood against the fence along Tamsin Lane, in a spot she had chosen for the morning sun, and she had built both of them herself long ago, a summer's work.
exclusions.B: When the snow melts, the Corder brothers will be back on the lane.
exclusions.C: What I thought about most, though, was the lane.
exclusions.E: Now the nights are turning cold, and until April the three hives are in my care.

support: Each time I heard the smack of a ball against the boards, I pictured the throw that would one day split a box wide open.
The smaller colony from the eaves still feels light when I tip its box, and on windy nights I lie awake wondering whether it has stored enough honey to last until spring.
WV12-P02.5.note: The narrator repeatedly pictures the hives being broken by stray balls and lies awake fearing the small colony will starve, which is plain worry, not criticism, amusement, admiration or nostalgia.

exclusions.A: In early October the birds will leave for the south, and the chimney will stand over the empty schoolyard until they return in May, as solid as it has always been.
exclusions.B: The masons who mended it chose lime mortar matched to the old, knowing that cheap cement would crack the soft brick and dry too smooth for a swift's claws.
exclusions.C: Whoever laid that brick built well enough for a furnace and, a hundred years on, well enough for six thousand swifts.
exclusions.D: The councillors read them through and voted to keep the chimney standing for the swifts.

support: A century after it was built, the chimney stands as straight and sound as the day its last brick was laid, the best-made thing on the hill.
Whoever laid that brick built well enough for a furnace and, a hundred years on, well enough for six thousand swifts.
WV12-P04.5.note: The writer calls the repaired chimney straight, sound and 'the best-made thing on the hill', praise read literally with no ironic or mournful reading available.
